Electrical discharge machining is frequently adopted for difficult-to-machine nickel‑chromium alloys such as Hastelloy C‑22 because conventional machining is often ineffective for these materials. (Nowicki et al. 2022) The physical and mechanical properties of the tool electrode directly influence process efficiency, machining accuracy, and surface roughness in EDM of such alloys. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Recent studies report a marked trend toward using graphite electrodes, motivated by low raw-material cost, good machinability, and high sublimation temperature. (Nowicki et al. 2022)

The two recent experimental studies on graphite electrodes report some agreement but also clear differences. Both studies emphasise the importance of electrode properties and machining parameters for MRR, TWR and Ra and both investigate POCO graphite grades with 1 µm and 10 µm grain sizes. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024) Nowicki et al. (2022) found that larger-grain graphite provides higher process efficiency (higher MRR) but at the cost of higher relative tool wear, while the smallest surface roughness was obtained with the finer-grained graphite; discharge current and pulse duration were identified as the main factors for MRR and Ra, and the time interval dominated relative tool wear. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Nowicki et al. (2024), by contrast, report that fine-grained graphite increases process efficiency and reduces tool wear, and they highlight the effect of detached graphite grains on discharge stability and process efficiency. (Nowicki et al. 2024) Thus the studies agree that grain size affects MRR, TWR and Ra and that machining parameters strongly influence outcomes, but they differ on whether larger or finer graphite grain yields the best combination of high efficiency and low tool wear. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)

Additional EDM studies support the importance of current and pulse duration: Nas & Kara found peak current to be the most influential factor for Ra and MRR, (Nas & Kara 2022) and Ramabalan et al. observed that current and pulse duration greatly affect electrode wear and surface edges. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) These findings align with the two graphite studies in identifying electrical parameters as primary drivers of machining performance. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)(Nas & Kara 2022)(Ramabalan et al. 2024)

Selective Laser Melting (SLM) produces near-full-density metallic parts by layer-wise melting and fusion of powder with a high-power laser, enabling near net-shape components with up to 99.9% relative density. (Yap et al. 2015) Metal AM, and SLM in particular, imparts unique microstructural features in steels—hierarchical subgrains and fine precipitates—that can enhance strength, wear and corrosion resistance compared with conventional routes, while also acting as an intrinsic heat treatment that induces in situ phase transformations and tempering phenomena. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

The cited studies generally agree that SLM of maraging steel produces very fine-scale microstructures and significant precipitation: Tan et al. report submicron grain sizes and needle-shaped Ni3X nanoprecipitates that explain age hardening and altered residual stress and anisotropy after heat treatment. (Tan et al. 2018) Haghdadi et al. similarly highlight hierarchical (sub)grains and fine precipitates as characteristic AM features that can improve corrosion and wear performance and act as an intrinsic heat treatment. (Haghdadi et al. 2020) Where the studies differ is in the specific effects of subsequent treatments and the corrosion outcomes: Godec et al. find that plasma nitriding without prior aging produces cracks in the compound layer and that prior heat treatments influence the morphology and protective quality of the nitride layer. (Godec et al. 2021) By contrast, Khan et al. focus on intercritical tempering that induces reversed austenite (noted along martensite lath boundaries) and report that this reversed austenite increases pitting potential and reduces corrosion current density in NaCl solution, i.e., it improves pitting resistance relative to as-printed, aged, and homogenized specimens. (Khan et al. 2022) Afkhami et al. review shows a different emphasis—identifying gaps in understanding of fatigue behavior of SLM steels—so it complements but does not directly address the microstructure–corrosion specifics treated in the other studies. (Afkhami et al. 2019)

(Khan et al. 2022) Finally, while many works emphasise improved static properties due to SLM microstructures, reviews note gaps in understanding of fatigue behaviour and the multiplicity of processing parameters affecting it, a topic addressed less directly by microstructure–corrosion studies.
